summary: When network configuration becomes invalid without any signal to local nodes, problems arise. This Best Current Practice specifies improvements to Customer Edge routers that mitigate them after IPv6 renumbering events. It updates RFC 7084.

eli5.summary: If a home network's address plan changes without warning, devices can keep using the old address. This document makes home routers react better and tell devices.

subtitle: Home and small-office IPv6 routers should stop leaving devices holding stale prefixes after a reboot or prefix change.

tldr.problem: When a Customer Edge router crashes and reboots, or an ISP hands out a new prefix, hosts on the local network can keep using stale configuration for an unacceptably long time, which causes connectivity problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds CE router requirements: do not automatically send DHCPv6-PD RELEASE on restart, keep IAIDs stable, never advertise lifetimes beyond the WAN-side ones, use shorter lifetimes (2700 and 5400 seconds), and explicitly deprecate stale prefixes with zero lifetimes.
tldr.outcome: CE routers recover from flash-renumbering events faster because hosts are told when old prefixes are no longer valid. It updates RFC 7084 and is a Best Current Practice.

facts.label: Stale prefix lifetimes
facts.value: Advertised with 0 Valid and Preferred Lifetime

today: RFC 9096 is a Best Current Practice and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 7084.

sections.title: The Stale Configuration Problem
sections.content:
Sometimes network configuration becomes invalid without any explicit signal. A typical case is a Customer Edge (CE) router that crashes and reboots without knowing which configuration it used before. Hosts on the local network then keep using stale information for an unacceptably long time, and connectivity breaks. The problem is documented in detail in RFC 8978.

RFC 9096 specifies improvements to CE routers for residential and small office scenarios. It sets recommendations for default behavior but does not rule out configuration knobs that let an operator or user deviate from them. It updates RFC 7084.
sections.eli5: When the router forgets its old address plan, the devices at home keep using the old one and stop working. This document is about fixing that.

sections.title: New and Changed CE Router Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements mainly target CE routers that learn prefixes through DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (DHCPv6-PD) on the WAN side and use SLAAC or DHCPv6 on the LAN side. They also do not rule out host-side improvements.

Two WAN-side requirements are added to RFC 7084: WPD-9 and WPD-10. LAN-side requirement L-13 is replaced, and L-15 and L-16 are added. The viz below lists them.
sections.eli5: The router gets a short list of new house rules: do not shout 'I quit' when restarting, keep the same ID, and tell everyone when an old address stops working.

sections.title: Staying Stable Across Restarts
sections.content:
Some CE routers automatically send DHCPv6-PD RELEASE messages when they restart. That can trigger a flash-renumbering scenario and the problems the RFC wants to avoid. So WPD-9 says CE routers SHOULD NOT automatically send such RELEASE messages on restart events.

Some popular CE routers pick new random Identity Association IDentifiers (IAIDs), for example each time a PPP session is established or the device reboots. RFC 8415 already requires the IAID for an IA to be consistent across DHCP client restarts. WPD-10 adds that CE routers MUST by default use a WAN-side IAID that is stable across router restarts, DHCPv6 client restarts and interface state changes, unless they use the IAID techniques of Section 4.5 of RFC 7844.
sections.eli5: The router should keep the same name tag every time it comes back, so the ISP still recognizes it and does not hand out a different address plan.

sections.title: Capping LAN-Side Lifetimes
sections.content:
Lifetimes advertised on the LAN side MUST NOT run past the remaining lifetimes of the matching WAN-side DHCPv6-PD prefixes. This applies to the "Preferred Lifetime" and "Valid Lifetime" of Prefix Information Options (PIOs) in Router Advertisements, and to the lifetimes in DHCPv6 IA Address and IA Prefix options. They must be adjusted dynamically so they never exceed the remaining WAN-side values. This matches RFC 8415, Section 6.3.

On top of that, CE routers SHOULD use shorter lifetimes. The Router Lifetime of Router Advertisements SHOULD be ND_PREFERRED_LIMIT. PIO and DHCPv6 preferred lifetimes SHOULD be the lesser of the remaining preferred lifetime and ND_PREFERRED_LIMIT, and valid lifetimes the lesser of the remaining valid lifetime and ND_VALID_LIMIT. The Route Lifetime of Route Information Options, and the lifetimes of RDNSS and DNSSL options, SHOULD be the lesser of the longest remaining valid lifetime and ND_VALID_LIMIT.

Recommended values are 2700 seconds (45 minutes) for ND_PREFERRED_LIMIT and 5400 seconds (90 minutes) for ND_VALID_LIMIT, which is twice the first to give hosts extra leeway. Shorter values are safe because later Router Advertisements and DHCPv6 renewals refresh the lifetimes, giving the same effective lifetime as the WAN side.
sections.eli5: The router should never promise a lease that lasts longer than the one it was given, and it should hand out short leases that get renewed often.

sections.title: Signaling Stale Configuration
sections.content:
With SLAAC on the LAN side, a CE router that advertises prefixes learned dynamically SHOULD record on stable storage the prefixes advertised in PIOs on each segment, plus the state of the "A" and "L" flags. After a change or after bootstrapping, any previously advertised prefix that is now stale MUST be advertised in PIOs with "Valid Lifetime" and "Preferred Lifetime" set to 0, with the "A" and "L" bits unchanged. This MUST go on for at least the Valid Lifetime used before, in unsolicited Router Advertisements, and MAY also use unicast RAs. If the recommended lifetimes are used, the stale prefix can simply be advertised for ND_VALID_LIMIT.

With DHCPv6 on the LAN side, the router SHOULD record address and prefix bindings on stable storage. If the prefix changed, or IA Prefix options arrive with 0 lifetimes, the router MUST answer Request, Renew and Rebind messages with IA Address or IA Prefix options for the stale prefixes, with both lifetimes set to 0, for at least the original valid lifetime or ND_VALID_LIMIT. It also initiates Reconfigure messages where possible. The storage requirements use SHOULD because they can be hard for some implementations.
sections.eli5: When an old address stops working, the router keeps announcing 'that one is dead' for a while, so even devices that missed the first shout get the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC discusses a problem that can arise where dynamic IPv6 prefixes are used, and proposes improvements to CE routers to reduce it for residential or small office networks. It does not introduce new security issues, so the security considerations of RFC 4861, RFC 4862, RFC 7084 and RFC 8415 apply. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: These changes do not open any new doors for bad guys, so the old safety rules still do the job.

viz.caption: REQUIREMENTS ADDED OR CHANGED BY RFC 9096

items.label: No automatic RELEASE
items.desc: SHOULD NOT automatically send DHCPv6-PD RELEASE messages on restart.

items.label: Stable IAID
items.desc: MUST by default use a WAN-side IAID that is stable across restarts and interface changes.

items.label: Signal stale information
items.desc: MUST signal stale configuration information as in Section 3.5 (replaces L-13 of RFC 7084).

items.label: Do not exceed WAN lifetimes
items.desc: MUST NOT advertise LAN lifetimes longer than the remaining WAN-side DHCPv6-PD lifetimes.

items.label: Cap option lifetimes
items.desc: SHOULD advertise capped SLAAC, IA Address and IA Prefix option lifetimes.
